Interpretation

What the result means

guided view

Stationarity and ESS viewed together

MDTest start ts=10374; ESS start ts=0; conservative reported start ts=10374.

The two analyses answer different questions. The MDTest branch screens stationarity-related block behavior; the ESS/IACT branch evaluates correlation-related sampling efficiency. Auto-compare reports both and currently uses the later start as its conservative combined start.

Why it matters: A large disagreement between the two starts is worth inspecting physically rather than hiding behind one scalar summary.

ESS/IACT correlation assessment

Selected statistical inefficiency g=1.029; effective sample count Neff=1.944e+04.

Statistical inefficiency measures the variance penalty from serial correlation in the retained series. Roughly, N correlated observations carry the mean-estimation information of about N/g independent observations under the assumptions of the estimator. The ESS scan chooses a candidate start that maximizes the retained effective sample count.

Why it matters: ESS/IACT addresses correlation and sampling efficiency. By itself it does not test whether the retained mean, variance, or distribution is stationary.

Mean-trend screen

No significant monotonic trend detected (p=0.2656).

The Mann-Kendall test is applied to the sequence of block means. A pass means the test did not detect a systematic monotonic drift at the chosen significance level; it is not proof that every form of nonstationarity is absent.

Why it matters: A continuing drift in the block means can bias an equilibrium average.

Dispersion-trend screen

No significant monotonic change in block dispersion detected (p=0.3028).

MDTest applies a Mann-Kendall trend screen to a block-level fluctuation proxy. This asks whether the size of the fluctuations is still changing with time, even when the mean itself may look settled.

Why it matters: A time-dependent fluctuation scale can bias variances and fluctuation-derived properties.

Block-mean normality screen

Block means are not rejected as non-normal (p=0.7145).

The Shapiro-Wilk test is applied to the block means. Passing means the available block means are compatible with the normality assumption at the chosen significance level; it does not prove that the underlying molecular observable itself is Gaussian.

Why it matters: Approximate normality of block means supports the Student-t uncertainty calculation used here.

Residual positive-correlation screen

No significant positive adjacent-block persistence detected (p=0.974).

The one-tailed von Neumann successive-difference diagnostic asks whether neighboring block means remain too similar. MDTest uses it as a local positive-correlation screen, not as a complete estimate of the full autocorrelation tail.

Why it matters: Residual block-to-block correlation means the chosen blocks may still be too short for reporting uncertainty.
